title: Concept Drills — States of Matter (Class 11 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.question: What single microscopic feature distinguishes solid, liquid and gas?
questions.solution: The balance between intermolecular ATTRACTION and molecular KE: solid — attraction dominates, particles vibrate in fixed positions; liquid — comparable, particles slide past each other but stay close; gas — KE dominates, particles fly independently. Heating tips the balance toward freedom; cooling toward order.

questions.question: At constant temperature, why does compressing a gas raise its pressure?
questions.solution: Constant T means constant molecular speed, so each collision delivers the same impulse. Compression packs the molecules closer — more collisions per second on each wall — raising pressure. P ∝ collision frequency ∝ number density at fixed speed.

questions.question: Under what conditions do real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour, and which assumption fails in each case?
questions.solution: High pressure: molecules occupy a significant fraction of the container — 'negligible molecular volume' fails, so the available volume is less than V (compressibility worse than ideal). Low temperature: molecular speeds drop, so intermolecular ATTRACTIONS have time to act — 'no forces' fails, pulling molecules together (compressibility better than ideal). Each condition breaks a different assumption.

questions.question: Why can a gas be liquefied by pressure alone below its critical temperature but not above it?
questions.solution: Liquefaction needs intermolecular attractions to overcome KE. Below Tc, the molecules' KE is low enough that pressure can push them into the liquid's attraction-dominated state. Above Tc, KE is too high — no pressure can hold molecules together as a liquid; the gas and liquid become indistinguishable (supercritical fluid).

questions.question: Why does a liquid in a closed container develop a fixed vapour pressure at a given temperature, and what does 'volatile' mean?
questions.solution: Evaporation and condensation run simultaneously; equilibrium is reached when rates equalise — the pressure of vapour at that balance is the vapour pressure, fixed by T (molecular energies) alone. A volatile liquid has weak intermolecular forces, so many molecules escape easily — high vapour pressure at low temperature.
